title: Reading the PRD
idea: A PRD (product requirements document) says what to build and why, in the product team's words. Read it to find the data, routes and rules your backend needs.

analogy.text: A client's brief to an architect: rooms, budget, deadline. It says what the building must do; the architect still chooses walls and wiring.
analogy.breaks: A PRD keeps changing while the product is built.

points: A PRD gives the goal, users, features, rules and what is out of scope.
A feature is often a user story: who, what and why in one sentence.
Nouns suggest data, verbs suggest routes, and rules suggest checks.
A PRD says what to build; how you build it is your design.

hero.title: One user story, read for the backend

parts.label: Who
parts.note: Says who may call. A member is logged in, so the route is secured.

parts.text: , I want to change my password
parts.label: What
parts.note: Names the action: one route, plus the data it receives.

parts.text: , so that my account stays safe
parts.label: Why
parts.note: States the goal. It hints at rules to check, such as hashing the new password (a one-way scramble, taught later).

code.title: The project's PRD
code.caption: The PRD for this project, trimmed to what the backend needs. Step through how a backend developer reads it.

walk.text: Two kinds of caller. The split decides which routes need a login.
Verbs such as register, verify and log in become routes. Nouns such as email become fields.
"Stay logged in" hints at a way to renew a login without the password.
A rule about time: each link needs an expiry stored beside its token.
A rule about safety: hash the password before saving it.
Operations are requirements too: monitors need a route to call.
Out of scope is binding. Do not build what this line lists.

pitfalls: Ask when a line is vague. "Verify email" could mean a link, a code, or both.
Do not guess a rule. Get exact numbers, such as how long a link lives.
Skip out-of-scope items: every extra feature is more code to test and secure.

quiz.q: The PRD says links in emails expire after 20 minutes. What must the backend store?
options: An expiry time stored with each token
Nothing: the email service enforces it
quiz.why: The server, not the email, decides if a link is still valid. It compares a stored expiry time with the current time.

takeaway: Read a PRD for nouns, verbs and rules; they become data, routes and checks.
